P A R T 1 Magic & Adventure Wishes, giants, secret caves and brave hearts. The Shepherd’s Treasure · Aladdin and the Magic Lamp · The Night Little Krishna Was Born · Gulliver’s Amazing Travels

L MA G I C & A DV E N T U R E · STO RY 1 The Shepherd’s Treasure A folk tale from old Persia ong, long ago, high on a mountain in Persia, there lived a kind shepherd named Ayaz. He had no house, only a snug little cave. He had no gold, only a flock of fluffy sheep and an old woollen blanket. But Ayaz was so kind and so wise that people walked for days just to ask him for advice. 7

News of the wise shepherd reached the palace. “A shepherd wiser than my ministers?” said the King. “I must see this for myself.” So the King took off his crown. He put on a dusty old cloak, climbed onto a grey mule and rode up the mountain, all alone. When he reached the cave, the sun was setting. “Hello, traveller!” called Ayaz. “You look tired. Come in and rest.” Ayaz gave the stranger cool water and shared his supper — just a little bread and cheese, but he gave the biggest piece away. That night the King slept on soft straw while the sheep said “baa” outside. In the morning, as the stranger climbed onto his mule, Ayaz bowed and said, “Thank you for visiting, Your Majesty.” 8

The King nearly fell off his mule! “How did you know I am the King?” Ayaz smiled. “A tired traveller looks at his dinner. But you looked at everything — the cave, the sheep, the way I spoke. Only someone who cares for a whole kingdom looks at the world like that.” The King laughed with delight. He brought Ayaz to the city and made him governor of a small town. Ayaz was fair and gentle, and soon everyone loved him. But not everyone was happy. The other governors grew jealous. “Your Majesty,” they whispered, “Ayaz carries a heavy iron chest everywhere he goes. He keeps it locked. We think it is full of stolen gold!” The King frowned. He called Ayaz to the palace. “Open your iron chest,” he said. Ayaz turned the key. Creeeak! The lid opened, and everyone leaned in to look… Inside there was no gold. No diamonds. Only an old, patched woollen blanket. “What is this?” asked the King. 9

“Your Majesty,” said Ayaz softly, “this is the blanket I used when I was a shepherd. I look at it every day, so I never forget where I came from. It keeps my heart humble.” The jealous governors turned as red as tomatoes. The King hugged Ayaz and made him the governor of the biggest city in the land. And every night, Ayaz still looked at his old blanket — and smiled. THE LESSON Stay kind and humble, no matter how big you grow. LET’S TALK! How did Ayaz know the stranger was the King? Why did Ayaz keep his old blanket? MAGIC WORD Humble — not showing off, even when you are important • • 10

O MA G I C & A DV E N T U R E · STO RY 2 Aladdin and the Magic Lamp A tale from the Arabian Nights nce upon a time, in a faraway city of domes and markets, there lived a boy named Aladdin. He was poor, but he was quick and curious, and he loved to explore every lane in the city. 11

One day, a tall stranger with a pointed beard stopped him. “Aladdin! I am your long-lost uncle,” he said with a sly smile. But he was not an uncle at all. He was a sneaky magician who wanted something only Aladdin could fetch. He led Aladdin out of the city to a lonely valley. He whispered a spell — FWOOSH! — and the ground opened to show stone steps going down, down, down. “Go into the cave,” said the magician. “Touch nothing except an old oil lamp. Bring the lamp to me.” He slipped a small ring onto Aladdin’s finger. “For luck,” he said. Aladdin climbed down. The cave was full of treasure trees with apples made of rubies and leaves made of emeralds! Aladdin found the dusty lamp and hurried back. “Give me the lamp first,” snapped the magician, “then I’ll pull you out.” “Help me out first,” said Aladdin. The magician stamped his foot in fury, and — BOOM! — the cave slammed shut. It was dark. Aladdin was scared. He rubbed his hands together — and rubbed the ring by mistake. POOF! A small, friendly genie appeared. “I am the Genie of the Ring! What do you wish?” 12

“Please take me home!” said Aladdin. In a blink, he was in his mother’s little kitchen. Aladdin’s mother began to clean the dusty lamp. As she rubbed it — WHOOOOSH! — golden smoke swirled up and up and became an enormous genie with a jolly smile. “I am the Genie of the Lamp!” he boomed. “Your wish is my command!” Aladdin did not wish for mountains of gold. He wished for food for his mother and their hungry neighbours. And with the Genie’s help, he became a kind and generous young man. One day he saw the Sultan’s daughter, Princess Badr, and she saw him. They became the best of friends, and soon they married and lived in a shining palace. 13

But the sneaky magician heard about the lamp. He dressed up as a lamp-seller. “New lamps for old!” he called outside the palace. A servant, not knowing the secret, swapped the magic lamp for a shiny new one! WHOOSH! The magician wished the palace and the princess far away to his own land. Aladdin did not give up. He rubbed his ring. “Genie of the Ring, take me to the Princess!” In a flash, he was there. Together, Aladdin and the Princess tricked the magician, grabbed the lamp and wished themselves home. The magician was sent far away, and Aladdin, the Princess and the jolly Genie lived happily and kindly ever after. THE LESSON Being brave and kind is more powerful than any magic. LET’S TALK! What would you wish for if you found a magic lamp? Why was it clever of Aladdin not to give away the lamp? MAGIC WORD Generous — happy to share what you have with others • • 14

L MA G I C & A DV E N T U R E · STO RY 3 The Night Little Krishna Was Born A story from ancient India ong ago, in the city of Mathura, there lived a gentle princess named Devaki and her kind husband, Vasudeva. But Devaki’s brother, King Kamsa, was a grumpy and cruel king. 15

One day a voice from the sky said, “Kamsa! Devaki’s eighth child will one day stop your cruel ways.” Kamsa was frightened. He locked Devaki and Vasudeva in a prison with heavy doors and big iron locks. The years went by, and they waited and prayed. Then, on a dark and stormy night, their eighth baby was born. He had skin the colour of rain clouds, and he smiled the sweetest smile. His name was Krishna. At that very moment, something magical happened. The prison guards yawned… and fell fast asleep. CLICK, CLICK, CLICK! The iron locks opened all by themselves, and the heavy doors swung wide. Vasudeva knew what to do. He placed baby Krishna in a little basket, lifted it onto his head and stepped out into the rain. 16

The Yamuna River was wild and deep. The rain poured down. But as Vasudeva walked into the water, the river grew calm and gentle, making a path for the baby. And a great serpent named Shesha rose up behind them and spread his wide hood like an umbrella, keeping Krishna safe and dry. On the other side of the river was the village of Gokul. There, a kind cowherd couple, Nanda and Yashoda, welcomed the baby with open arms. Vasudeva kissed his son goodbye and hurried back before the guards woke up. In the morning, King Kamsa stormed into the prison. But the special baby was already far away, safe and loved. In Gokul, little Krishna grew up happy and cheeky. He played the flute so sweetly that cows came dancing. He loved butter so 17

much that he sneaked it from pots when no one was looking! And he grew up to be brave and wise, and to stand up for what was right. Even today, on the night of his birthday, called Janmashtami, families all over the world sing songs, share sweets and remember the stormy night when love kept a little baby safe. THE LESSON Love and goodness always find a way. LET’S TALK! What magical things happened on the night Krishna was born? Who helped keep baby Krishna safe? MAGIC WORD Protect — to keep someone safe from harm • • 18

L MA G I C & A DV E N T U R E · STO RY 4 Gulliver’s Amazing Travels Adapted from the classic by Jonathan Swift emuel Gulliver was a ship’s doctor who loved to travel the seas. One day, a terrible storm crashed his ship onto the rocks. Gulliver swam and swam until he reached a sandy beach, and there he fell fast asleep. When he woke up, he could not move! Hundreds of tiny ropes held him down. And standing on his chest was a man… no bigger than a pencil! 19

Gulliver had landed in Lilliput, where everyone was tiny. The Lilliputians were scared of the giant. But Gulliver spoke gently and never stomped on anyone, and soon they became friends. It took three hundred tiny cooks to make Gulliver’s dinner. Six hundred tiny beds were sewn together to make his mattress. The children climbed into his pockets and slid down his arms like a slide! The Lilliputians had a very silly problem. They were fighting with the island next door, Blefuscu — all because they could not agree which end of a boiled egg to crack first: the big end or the little end! 20

Gulliver waded into the sea and pulled the enemy’s tiny ships away with a rope, so no one could fight. “It’s only an egg,” he told them kindly. “Crack it any way you like!” After many adventures, Gulliver built a boat and sailed home. But he could not stay still for long. Soon he set off again — and a storm blew him to another strange land called Brobdingnag. This time, everything was ENORMOUS! The grass was as tall as trees. The farmer who found him was as tall as a tower. Now Gulliver was the tiny one! A kind farm girl named Glumdalclitch looked after him. She made him a bed in a doll’s cradle and carried him everywhere in a little box. A bee the size of a bird buzzed past him. A raindrop was as big as a bucket of water! The Queen of the giants loved listening to Gulliver’s stories. But one day, a giant eagle picked up his little box and flew high over the sea. Then — SPLASH! — it dropped him into the waves, and a passing ship rescued him. At last, Gulliver came home to his family. “I have been a giant and I have been tiny,” he said. “And I learned that everyone, big or small, deserves to be treated kindly.” 21

THE LESSON Big or small, everyone deserves kindness and respect. LET’S TALK! Would you rather visit the land of tiny people or the land of giants? Why? Why was the egg fight so silly? MAGIC WORD Respect — treating others the way you would like to be treated The End • • 22

B C L E V E R A N I MA L S · STO RY 5 The Monkey and the Crocodile A Panchatantra tale from India y a sparkling river stood a tall rose-apple tree covered with sweet, pink fruit. In that tree lived a cheerful monkey named Kavi. 24

One sunny day, a big crocodile named Chandra swam up to the riverbank. “Hello up there!” he called. “Those fruits look delicious.” “They are!” said Kavi, and he tossed down a handful. Chandra munched them happily. From that day on, the monkey and the crocodile became friends. Every day Kavi shared his fruit, and every day Chandra told him stories about the river. Chandra took some rose-apples home to his wife. She loved them. But then she had a greedy idea. “If the fruit is this sweet,” she said, “imagine how sweet that monkey’s heart must be! Bring me his heart for dinner.” Chandra did not want to hurt his friend. But his wife would not stop asking. So the next day he said, “Kavi, my wife wants to meet you. Climb on my back and I’ll take you across the river.” Kavi jumped onto Chandra’s back, and off they went. But in the middle of the deep river, Chandra said sadly, “I’m sorry, Kavi. My wife wants to eat your heart.” 25

Kavi’s heart went thump-thump-thump! He was in the middle of the river and he could not swim. But he stayed calm and thought fast. “Oh, Chandra!” he said. “Why didn’t you tell me before? We monkeys keep our hearts safely in the tree! Take me back, and I’ll fetch it for you.” The silly crocodile turned around and swam back to the tree. The moment they reached the bank, Kavi leapt — WHOOSH! — to the highest branch. “Where is your heart?” called Chandra. 26

Kavi laughed. “My heart is right here in my chest, where it has always been! Nobody can keep their heart in a tree. A real friend would never try to trick a friend.” Chandra hung his head. “You are right, Kavi. I am sorry.” Kavi thought for a moment. “If you truly want to be friends,” he said, “then from now on, be honest with me. And tell your wife I will send her rose-apples — only rose-apples!” From that day, Chandra always told the truth, and Kavi tossed down fruit every morning. And the crocodile’s wife learned that rose-apples are very tasty indeed. THE LESSON When you’re in trouble, stay calm and think. And real friends are always honest. LET’S TALK! How did Kavi escape? What makes someone a good friend? MAGIC WORD Calm — quiet and steady, not panicking • • 27

I C L E V E R A N I MA L S · STO RY 6 The Lion and the Mouse A fable by Aesop, from ancient Greece n the middle of a sunny grassland, a mighty lion was having an afternoon nap. His big tail swished. His big nose snored: ZZZZ… ZZZZ… A tiny mouse came scurrying by. She was in such a hurry that she ran right over the lion’s nose! 28

The lion woke up with a ROAR! He trapped the mouse under his huge paw. “How dare you wake me!” he growled. “I shall eat you for a snack!” “Please, King Lion!” squeaked the mouse. “Let me go! One day, I might be able to help you.” The lion laughed so hard his whiskers wobbled. “YOU? Help ME? You are so tiny!” But the mouse had made him laugh, so he lifted his paw. “Off you go, little one.” “Thank you!” said the mouse. “I won’t forget.” A few days later, the lion was walking through the forest when — WHOOSH! — a hunter’s net fell over him. The lion roared and pulled and twisted. But the more he struggled, the tighter the ropes became. 29

His roars echoed through the trees. Far away, the little mouse heard them. “That’s my friend!” she said, and she ran as fast as her little legs could carry her. “Don’t worry, King Lion,” she said. “I’m here!” And she began to nibble the ropes. Nibble, nibble, nibble. Snip! One rope broke. Nibble, nibble, nibble. Snip! Another rope broke. Soon there was a hole big enough for the lion to climb out. He was free! The lion looked down at the tiny mouse. “I laughed at you,” he said quietly. “But you saved my life. Thank you, my friend.” From that day on, the lion and the mouse were the best of friends. And whenever anyone said the mouse was too small to matter, the lion would give a friendly ROAR and say, “Small friends can do BIG things!” THE LESSON No act of kindness is ever wasted — and nobody is too small to help. LET’S TALK! Why did the lion let the mouse go? Have you ever helped someone bigger than you? MAGIC WORD Grateful — feeling thankful when someone helps you • • 30

H C L E V E R A N I MA L S · STO RY 7 The Tortoise and the Hare A fable by Aesop, from ancient Greece are was the fastest animal in the meadow, and he never stopped telling everyone about it. “I’m the speediest! I’m the zoomiest! Nobody can beat me!” One morning he saw Tortoise walking slowly along the path. Step… step… step. “Ha!” laughed Hare. “You’re so slow, a snail could beat you!” 31

Tortoise blinked. “Maybe I am slow,” he said. “But I will race you.” All the animals gasped. Then they giggled. A race? Tortoise against Hare? Owl drew a starting line. Fox put a red flag at the finish, far away past the big oak tree. “Ready… steady… GO!” WHOOSH! Hare shot off like a rocket. Dust flew everywhere. Tortoise began to walk. Step… step… step. Soon Hare was so far ahead that he could not even see Tortoise. “This is too easy,” he yawned. “I have plenty of time for a little nap.” He lay down in the cool shade of the oak tree and closed his eyes. 32

Tortoise kept going. Step… step… step. His legs were tired. The sun was hot. But he did not stop. Step… step… step. He walked past the sleeping Hare, very quietly. Suddenly Hare woke up. He looked around. Where was Tortoise? Then he saw him — right next to the finish line! Hare jumped up and ran faster than he had ever run before. ZOOM! ZOOM! ZOOM! But it was too late. Tortoise stepped over the finish line, and all the animals cheered, “Hooray for Tortoise!” Hare was out of breath and very embarrassed. “How did you win?” he panted. “I’m so much faster!” Tortoise smiled a slow, kind smile. “You were fast,” he said. “But I never stopped. A little step every day, and you’ll get there in the end.” THE LESSON Slow and steady wins the race. Keep going, one small step at a time. LET’S TALK! What mistake did Hare make? What is something you get better at a little every day? MAGIC WORD Steady — doing something evenly, without stopping • • 33

I C L E V E R A N I MA L S · STO RY 8 The Thirsty Crow A fable told in India and Greece t was the hottest day of the summer. The sun was blazing. The ponds had dried up, and the grass was brown and crunchy. A little black crow flew over the fields. “Caw! Caw! I’m so thirsty,” he croaked. “I must find some water.” 34

He flew over the village. He flew over the hills. At last, in a garden, he saw a tall clay pot. He landed on its edge and peeked inside. There was water! But only a little, right at the very bottom. The crow pushed his beak into the pot. It was too deep. He stretched his neck. Still too deep! He tried to tip the pot over, but it was far too heavy. “Oh dear,” sighed the crow. Many birds would have given up and flown away. But the crow sat down and thought. And thought. And thought. Then he saw some small pebbles lying on the ground. “I have an idea!” he cawed. 35

He picked up a pebble in his beak and dropped it into the pot. Plop! He picked up another. Plop! And another. Plop! Plop! Plop! With every pebble, the water rose a little higher. Plop… it rose. Plop… it rose higher. Plop… higher still! At last the water came all the way up to the top of the pot. The crow dipped his beak and drank and drank the cool, fresh water. “Aaaah! Caw-caw-wonderful!” Then he called to his thirsty friends. “Come and drink! And bring your pebbles!” And soon a whole flock of happy birds were sipping from the pot together. THE LESSON Don’t give up. Think hard — there is almost always a clever way. LET’S TALK! What did the crow do when his beak couldn’t reach? Can you think of another way the crow could get the water? MAGIC WORD Idea — a new thought about how to do something • • 36

D C L E V E R A N I MA L S · STO RY 9 The Clever Rabbit and the Lion A Panchatantra tale from India eep in the forest lived a huge, hungry lion called Bhasuraka. Every day he chased the animals and roared so loudly that the leaves shook off the trees. The animals were tired of running and hiding. So they held a meeting. Deer, bear, jackal, monkey and rabbit all sat in a circle. 37

“Let’s make a deal with the lion,” said old Elephant. “If he stops chasing us, we will send one animal to him every day.” The lion agreed. But nobody was happy with the plan. And one day it was the little rabbit’s turn. The rabbit hopped along the path very, very slowly, thinking hard. By the time he reached the lion, it was long past lunchtime. “You’re LATE!” roared the lion. “And you’re TINY!” “I’m sorry, Your Majesty,” said the rabbit, bowing. “Five rabbits set off to see you. But on the way, another lion stopped us. He said HE is the king of this forest!” “ANOTHER lion?” roared Bhasuraka. “There can’t be another king! Show him to me!” The rabbit led him to an old, deep well. “He lives down there, Your Majesty.” 38

The lion peered over the edge. Down in the water he saw a big, angry lion staring back at him! It was only his own reflection, but the lion did not know that. He roared. “ROAAAR!” And from the well came an echo: “ROAAAR!” “How dare you roar at ME!” The furious lion jumped into the well to fight — SPLASH! — and he could not climb out. The clever rabbit hopped back to the forest. “The lion won’t bother us anymore!” The animals cheered and danced, and they made the little rabbit the Hero of the Forest. 39

THE LESSON Being clever can be stronger than being big. LET’S TALK! What did the lion really see in the well? How did the rabbit use his brain instead of his strength? MAGIC WORD Reflection — the picture of yourself you see in water or a mirror The End • • 40

O C L E V E R A N I MA L S · STO RY 1 0 The Goose with the Golden Eggs A fable by Aesop, from ancient Greece nce there was a farmer and his wife who lived in a little cottage with a red roof. They had a cow, two goats and a white goose named Goldie. 41

One morning, the farmer went to Goldie’s nest to collect an egg. He picked it up — and nearly dropped it! The egg was bright, shiny, heavy GOLD! “Look!” he shouted. His wife came running. They bit it. They weighed it. It really was gold! The next morning, there was another golden egg. And the next morning, another! Every single day, Goldie laid one golden egg. The farmer and his wife sold the eggs and bought new clothes, a new roof and plenty of food. They were very happy. At first. But soon, one egg a day was not enough. “Why should we wait?” grumbled the farmer. “If Goldie makes golden eggs, she must be full of gold inside! Let’s squeeze her and get it all at once!” “Yes!” said his wife. “Let’s get all the gold today!” So they chased Goldie around the yard. “Come here, goosey!” The goose flapped and honked. HONK! HONK! They grabbed at her feathers. They shouted and shoved. 42

Goldie was so frightened that she spread her wings and flew — up, up, over the red roof, over the trees, far, far away. The farmer and his wife stood in the empty yard. There were no more golden eggs. Not one. “Oh dear,” said the farmer sadly. “We had a golden egg every day, and we wanted everything at once. Now we have nothing.” From that day on, they worked hard in their fields. And they never forgot the lesson of Goldie the goose. 43

THE LESSON Be patient and be thankful. Wanting everything at once can mean losing it all. LET’S TALK! Why did Goldie fly away? What does it mean to be patient? MAGIC WORD Greedy — wanting much more than you need The End • • 44

P A R T 3 Wise & Witty Funny tricks and smart answers from the wisest people in the land. Mullah Nasrudin and the Magic Mango · Birbal Counts the Crows · Tenali Raman and the Garden Thieves · The Blind Men and the Elephant

I W I S E & W I T T Y · STO RY 1 1 Mullah Nasrudin and the Magic Mango A funny tale of Mullah Nasrudin n the busy town of Baltistan, high among the mountains, there lived a funny man called Mullah Nasrudin. He had a big turban, a bushy beard and a little grey donkey who followed him everywhere. 46

One morning, Nasrudin went to the market. It was full of colours and smells — spices, sweets, carpets and fruit. Then he saw a fruit cart with a big sign: MAGIC MANGOES! One bite, one wish! “A wish!” said Nasrudin, rubbing his hands. He bought the biggest, juiciest mango on the cart. He held it up high. Everyone in the market stopped to watch. He took a huge, dramatic bite. CHOMP! Nothing happened. No genie. No sparkles. No magic. Just mango juice dripping down his beard. The fruit seller looked worried. The crowd began to giggle. But Nasrudin was not the kind of man who gave up. He stood up tall and shouted, “Oh, magical mango! I wish to be the greatest juggler in the world!” 47

Then he grabbed three mangoes and threw them in the air. Up, up, up! He caught one — oops! — dropped one on his donkey’s head — BONK! — and caught the last one on his big nose! The crowd roared with laughter. Nasrudin grinned and tried again. Up went the mangoes. Round and round they flew. Then he added an orange. And a melon! He hopped on one foot. He juggled standing on his donkey! Everyone clapped and cheered. Even the donkey hee-hawed. A circus owner was passing by. “Magnificent!” he cried. “Will you be the star of my circus?” So Nasrudin became the funniest juggler the town had ever seen. And whenever children asked him, “Was it really a magic 48

mango?” Nasrudin would wink and say, “The mango was just a mango. The magic was in trying — and in making everyone laugh!” THE LESSON The real magic is in trying, practising and sharing joy. LET’S TALK! Was the mango really magic? What would you like to get better at? MAGIC WORD Practise — doing something again and again to get better • • 49

L W I S E & W I T T Y · STO RY 1 2 Birbal Counts the Crows A tale of Akbar and Birbal from India ong ago, Emperor Akbar ruled India from a grand palace. He loved puzzles and riddles, and his favourite advisor was a clever man named Birbal, who could answer any question with a smile. One morning, Akbar and Birbal were walking in the palace garden. Crows were cawing on every wall and every roof. Caw! Caw! Caw! 50

Akbar had an idea for a tricky puzzle. “Birbal,” he said, “tell me, how many crows are there in my whole city?” The ministers smiled to each other. Surely nobody could answer that! There were thousands of roofs and thousands of trees. Birbal thought for just a moment. Then he bowed. “Your Majesty, there are exactly ninety-five thousand, four hundred and sixty-three crows in the city.” Akbar raised his eyebrows. “Exactly? And what if I ask my soldiers to count, and there are more?” “Then, Your Majesty,” said Birbal, “some crows must be visiting their cousins from other cities.” 51

The ministers giggled. Akbar tried not to smile. “And if there are fewer?” “Then some of our crows must have gone to visit their relatives in other cities!” Akbar burst out laughing. He laughed so much that he had to hold his tummy. “Birbal, you always have an answer!” He gave Birbal a gift of gold coins. And the crows? They just kept cawing on the palace roof — caw! caw! caw! — as if they were laughing too. THE LESSON A quick mind and a sense of humour can solve even impossible puzzles. LET’S TALK! Why couldn’t anyone check Birbal’s answer? Can you make up a funny answer to a tricky question? MAGIC WORD Advisor — someone who gives helpful ideas and advice • • 52

T W I S E & W I T T Y · STO RY 1 3 Tenali Raman and the Garden Thieves A tale of Tenali Raman from South India enali Raman was the cleverest poet in the kingdom of King Krishnadevaraya. He lived in a small house with a beautiful garden full of mango trees, banana plants and bright flowers. 53

That summer, there was very little rain. Every day, Tenali had to pull bucket after bucket of water from the deep well to water his thirsty garden. It was very hard work. One evening, as he sat by the window, Tenali saw something move behind the bushes. It was three thieves! They were whispering, “When everyone is asleep, we’ll sneak into the house and steal all the treasure!” Tenali smiled. He had an idea. He called loudly to his wife, so the thieves could hear. “Wife! These days there are so many thieves around. Let’s put all our gold and jewels in this big box and drop it into the well. No one will ever find it there!” His wife understood the plan at once. Together, they filled a big box with heavy stones, closed the lid and — SPLASH! — dropped it into the well. Then they went to bed, giggling quietly. The thieves rubbed their hands. “The treasure is in the well! Let’s pull out all the water and grab the box!” 54

All night long, the thieves pulled up bucket after bucket of water. Heave! Splash! Heave! Splash! They poured it out on the ground — right onto Tenali’s garden. Every tree and every flower drank and drank. At last, just as the sun came up, the thieves reached the box. They broke it open. Stones! Only stones! At that moment, Tenali leaned out of the window. “Thank you, my friends!” he called. “My garden has never been watered so well!” The thieves were so embarrassed that they ran away and never came back. And Tenali’s garden bloomed all summer long. 55

THE LESSON Using your brain can turn a problem into a surprise helper. LET’S TALK! How did Tenali trick the thieves? Who really did the hard work in the garden? MAGIC WORD Clever — quick at thinking and understanding The End • • 56

I W I S E & W I T T Y · STO RY 1 4 The Blind Men and the Elephant A wisdom tale from India n a small village lived six friends who could not see with their eyes. But they could see with their hands, their ears and their clever minds. 57

One day, a man brought an elephant to the village. “An elephant!” said the friends. “We have heard of elephants, but we have never met one. Let’s find out what it is like!” The first friend touched the elephant’s big, flat side. “An elephant is like a wall!” he said. The second friend touched a long, curved tusk. “No, an elephant is like a spear!” The third friend held the wiggly trunk. “You’re both wrong! An elephant is like a snake!” The fourth friend hugged a thick leg. “Nonsense! An elephant is like a tree!” The fifth friend felt a flapping ear. “An elephant is like a big fan!” The sixth friend caught the swishy tail. “Silly! An elephant is like a rope!” 58

Wall! Spear! Snake! Tree! Fan! Rope! The six friends argued louder and louder. The elephant just flapped its ears and said, “Hrmmmph?” A wise old woman walking by began to laugh. “Friends, friends! You are all right, and you are all wrong. Each of you touched only one part. An elephant has ALL of those parts. Put your ideas together, and you will know the whole elephant.” The six friends were quiet. Then they laughed too. They shared what each of them had felt, and together they imagined the whole wonderful elephant: tall as a wall, with legs like trees, a trunk like a snake, tusks like spears, ears like fans and a tail like a rope. “Next time,” said the first friend, “let’s listen before we argue!” 59

THE LESSON Everyone sees a different part of the truth. Listen to each other. LET’S TALK! Why did each friend think the elephant was something different? Why is it good to listen to other people’s ideas? MAGIC WORD Listen — paying careful attention to what someone says The End • • 60
P A R T 4 Brand-New Bedtime Tales Two new stories to snuggle up with at the end of the day. Chotu the Little Seed · Tara and the Littlest Star

C B RA N D - N E W B E DT I M E TA L E S · STO RY 1 5 Chotu the Little Seed A brand-new story by Veer Sukhadiya hotu was a tiny seed. He was so small that he could sit on the tip of a ladybird’s nose. One spring morning, a girl named Meera dug a little hole in her garden. She placed Chotu inside, covered him with soft, dark soil and gave him a sprinkle of water. “Grow big and strong, little seed,” she whispered. 62

Down in the dark, Chotu looked up at the soil. “I want to be a big tree RIGHT NOW!” he said. He pushed and he pushed. But nothing happened. The next day, Meera came to look. There was nothing but brown earth. The next day, still nothing. A week went by. “Maybe my seed isn’t growing,” Meera said sadly. But she kept watering him, a little every day. What Meera could not see was that under the ground, Chotu WAS growing. Every day, a tiny root wiggled a little deeper. Every day, it grew a little longer. A worm stopped by. “What are you doing?” it asked. “I’m growing roots,” said Chotu. “Roots are slow. Nobody can see them. But they will hold me up when I’m tall.” 63

One morning — POP! — a tiny green shoot peeked out of the soil. “Chotu!” cried Meera. “You’re growing!” After that, Chotu grew a little every single day. Two leaves. Four leaves. Ten leaves! A thin little trunk. Branches that reached for the sun. The summer wind blew hard, but Chotu did not fall over, because his roots held him tight. The rain poured down, but Chotu drank it up and grew even stronger. Years passed. Meera grew taller, and so did Chotu. He grew into a huge mango tree with branches wide enough for a swing and shade big enough for a picnic. Now Meera’s children play under Chotu’s branches and eat his sweet mangoes. And sometimes, when the wind blows, the leaves seem to whisper: “A little bit every day… a little bit every day…” THE LESSON Big things grow from small steps. Be patient — your roots are growing. LET’S TALK! What was Chotu doing when nobody could see him? What small thing could you do every day to grow? MAGIC WORD Patient — able to wait calmly for something good • • 64

E B RA N D - N E W B E DT I M E TA L E S · STO RY 1 6 Tara and the Littlest Star A brand-new story by Veer Sukhadiya very night, before she went to sleep, a little girl named Tara looked out of her window and said goodnight to the stars. There was the big bright star, the twinkly blue star and the star that looked like a diamond. And right at the edge of the sky, there was one very small star. It was so tiny that Tara had to squint to see it. 65

“Goodnight, Littlest Star,” Tara whispered. The Littlest Star felt shy. “Why does she say goodnight to me?” it wondered. “I’m the smallest. I’m the dimmest. My light doesn’t matter.” One night, big grey clouds rolled across the sky. They covered the big bright star. They covered the twinkly blue star. They covered the diamond star. The whole sky went dark. Far out on the sea, a little fishing boat was sailing home. The fisherman, Tara’s grandfather, looked up. “Where are the stars?” he said. “I can’t find my way home in the dark.” But right at the edge of the sky, there was one small gap in the clouds. And through that gap, the Littlest Star was shining. 66

“I’m so small,” it thought. “But I must try.” So it took a deep breath and shone as brightly as it could. Twinkle… twinkle… TWINKLE! Grandfather saw the little light. “There!” he said. “That star is over our village!” He steered his boat towards it, all the way home to the harbour. The next morning, Grandfather told Tara all about the little star that had guided him home. That night, when the sky was clear again, Tara leaned out of her window. She looked past the big bright star and the twinkly blue star, right to the edge of the sky. “Thank you, Littlest Star,” she whispered. “You may be small, but you shine just right.” And the Littlest Star twinkled the happiest twinkle in the whole wide sky. Goodnight. THE LESSON You don’t have to be the biggest to make a big difference. Just shine as you are. LET’S TALK! How did the Littlest Star help Grandfather? What makes YOU shine? MAGIC WORD Guide — to show someone the way • • 67
